question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
In this cold weather, / there's nothing / like good / cup of coffee.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. like good.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The complete sentence reads "In this cold weather, there's nothing like good cup of coffee." The phrase "like good cup of coffee" is missing the indefinite article "a" before the singular countable noun phrase "good cup of coffee".

• Rule — Articles with singular countable nouns: A singular countable noun (or a noun phrase built around one, such as "good cup of coffee") must always be preceded by an article (a/an/the) or another determiner. The correct segment should read "like a good cup of coffee".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "In this cold weather" is correct; it is a well-formed prepositional phrase of time/circumstance.

• Option 3: "cup of coffee" is grammatically fine as a noun phrase in itself (the missing article belongs with segment 2, not here).

• Option 4: "there's nothing" is a correct contraction of "there is nothing" and needs no correction.

NOTE

• Common SSC trap: missing articles before singular countable nouns, e.g. "he is honest man" (should be "an honest man"), "she bought new car" (should be "a new car").

• The idiomatic expression is "There's nothing like a good cup of coffee/tea", commonly used to praise something as the best of its kind.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
The general's address / was applauds / by all sections / of society.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was applauds.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The general's address was applauds by all sections of society" is in the passive voice, which requires the structure Subject + was/were + Verb (V3/past participle) + by + agent.

• Rule — Passive voice with "was": After the auxiliary "was", the main verb must be in its past participle (V3) form, not the plain present-tense/plural form. Here, "applauds" is incorrect; it should be "applauded" (V3 of applaud).

• Corrected segment: "was applauded".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "by all sections" is correct; "by + agent" is the standard passive-voice structure.

• Option 3: "of society." is correct; it correctly completes the noun phrase "all sections of society".

• Option 4: "the general's address" is correct; the possessive 's is properly used and the noun phrase is the grammatical subject of the passive sentence.

NOTE

• Passive voice verb forms always use V3, e.g. is/are/was/were + V3, has/have/had been + V3, will be + V3.

• Common SSC error type: using the base form or plural form of the verb instead of the past participle after was/were/is/are/been, e.g. "was break" instead of "was broken".

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
There's an quiet street down the left that you can use for your dance practice.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. There's an quiet street.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "There's an quiet street" wrongly uses the article "an" before "quiet".

• Rule — a vs an: "A" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound, and "an" before words beginning with a vowel sound. The word "quiet" begins with the consonant sound /kw/ (as in "quick"), so it must take "a", not "an".

• Corrected segment: "There's a quiet street".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "down the left" is correct; it is a standard prepositional phrase of direction.

• Option 2: "that you can use" is correct; it is a properly formed relative clause modifying "street".

• Option 4: "for your dance practice" is correct; it correctly completes the sentence with a prepositional phrase of purpose.

NOTE

• Other words that sound like they should take "an" but actually take "a" because of their consonant sound: university, European, one-eyed, unique, useful (all begin with the /y/ sound).

• Conversely, words like hour, honest, heir take "an" because the initial "h" is silent.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
A part / of an / apple is / rotten.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. of an.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "of an" wrongly uses the indefinite article "an" before "apple". The sentence is talking about one particular, specific apple — a definite item, one part of which is rotten — so it needs the definite article "the", not the indefinite article "an".

• Rule — a/an vs the: The indefinite article a/an is used for a non-specific, any-one-of-a-class noun, whereas the definite article the is used when the noun refers to one specific, identifiable thing. Since the sentence points to a specific apple (the one with a rotten part), the correct form is "a part of the apple".

• Corrected segment: "of the", giving "A part of the apple is rotten."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "apple is" is grammatically fine on its own; the noun "apple" (once correctly preceded by "the") correctly agrees with the singular verb "is".

• Option 3: "A part" is correct; "a" is properly used before the singular countable noun "part".

• Option 4: "rotten." is correct; it is the correct predicate adjective completing the sentence.

NOTE

• Whenever a sentence refers to "a part/portion/piece of" one specific, already-identified object, the noun that follows normally takes "the", e.g. "a part of the story", "a slice of the cake", "a corner of the room".

• Contrast this with a genuinely generic reference, where the indefinite article is correct, e.g. "He ate a part of an apple" (any apple, unspecified) versus "A part of the apple (that he was eating) was rotten" (one specific apple).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives. They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change and create homes for thousands of species of plants and animals. (3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss. When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity. A billion is a big number, but we know we can do it together. (5)________ the planet by planting your tree today. This can protect and restore forests for future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives." The correct preposition is "in", giving "benefits in our everyday lives"**, meaning the benefits occur/exist within the context of daily life.

• Rule — Preposition collocation: The phrase "benefits in [someone's] life/lives" is the standard, idiomatic collocation used to describe advantages that apply within a sphere of life or activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "to" is incorrect; "benefits to our lives" is not the natural collocation used here (it would suggest benefits directed at, rather than existing within, our lives).

• Option 3: "for" is incorrect; "for" would suggest purpose/beneficiary and does not fit the intended meaning of benefits occurring within daily life.

• Option 4: "with" is incorrect; "with" does not logically connect "benefits" and "our everyday lives" here.

NOTE

• Preposition usage is largely governed by fixed collocation in English and must be learnt through practice; common tested pairs include "benefit from", "believe in", "depend on", "good at".

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (and often the surrounding sentences) before choosing a preposition, since meaning determines the correct one.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives. They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change and create homes for thousands of species of plants and animals. (3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss. When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity. A billion is a big number, but we know we can do it together. (5)________ the planet by planting your tree today. This can protect and restore forests for future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. curb.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is in **"They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change...". The correct word is "curb", meaning to control, restrain, or keep something (usually something negative) in check. "Help curb climate change"** means to help control/limit climate change.

• Rule — Word choice by meaning/collocation: The verb after "help" must logically fit with a large-scale problem like climate change; "curb" is the standard collocation used in environmental writing ("curb emissions", "curb climate change", "curb pollution").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "crib" is incorrect; "crib" means a baby's cot or (informally) to complain/copy — it does not fit the context of climate change.

• Option 2: "cut" is incorrect; while trees can reduce carbon, "help cut climate change" is not idiomatic — "cut emissions" would work, but not "cut climate change" itself.

• Option 4: "crust" is incorrect; "crust" is a noun (the outer layer of something, e.g. the earth's crust or bread's crust) and cannot function as a verb after "help".

NOTE

• Common collocations in environment-related passages: curb emissions, mitigate climate change, combat pollution, conserve resources, restore forests, offset carbon.

• Be alert to words that sound similar (crib/curb/crust/cut) — cloze questions frequently test such close look-alikes.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives. They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change and create homes for thousands of species of plants and animals. (3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss. When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity. A billion is a big number, but we know we can do it together. (5)________ the planet by planting your tree today. This can protect and restore forests for future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Planting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank begins a new sentence: **"(3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss." Here the blank must supply the subject of the sentence, and the verb that follows is "can help"**.

• Rule — Gerund as subject: A gerund (verb + -ing) can function as the subject of a sentence when the action itself (not a person) is being discussed. "Planting a billion trees" is a gerund phrase acting as the subject, correctly followed by the singular verb "can help".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "In planting" is incorrect; adding the preposition "In" before the gerund makes it a prepositional phrase, leaving the sentence without a proper subject for "can help".

• Option 2: "With planting" is incorrect for the same reason — it turns the gerund phrase into a prepositional phrase rather than a subject.

• Option 3: "By planting" is incorrect; "by" would only be appropriate if there were an earlier main clause for it to attach to (e.g., "We can save the Earth by planting..."), but here the blank must start a fresh, independent sentence.

NOTE

• A gerund phrase used as a subject always takes a singular verb, e.g. "Reading books improves vocabulary", "Planting trees helps the environment".

• Watch for cloze blanks at the start of a sentence — they usually require either a subject (noun/gerund) or a sentence-initial connector, never a bare preposition immediately before the main verb slot.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives. They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change and create homes for thousands of species of plants and animals. (3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss. When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity. A billion is a big number, but we know we can do it together. (5)________ the planet by planting your tree today. This can protect and restore forests for future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. conserve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is in **"When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity." The correct word is "conserve", meaning to protect something from harm, loss, or wasteful use. "Restore and conserve critical forests"** is a natural, commonly used pair describing environmental protection.

• Rule — Parallel meaning in a paired verb structure: When two verbs are joined by "and" in a list of related actions (here, "restore and ___"), the missing verb should carry a similar, complementary positive meaning, not an opposite or unrelated one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sabotage" is incorrect; it means to deliberately damage or destroy, the opposite of the intended positive meaning.

• Option 3: "observe" is incorrect; it means to watch or notice, which does not fit the active, protective sense required alongside "restore".

• Option 4: "curtail" is incorrect; it means to reduce or cut short, which does not logically pair with "restore" in a positive environmental context.

NOTE

• Common positive environment-related verb pairs: restore and conserve, protect and preserve, sustain and support.

• Always check whether the missing word must match (parallel) or contrast with a nearby word — this is a frequent cloze-passage trick in SSC exams.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees provide so many benefits (1)____ our everyday lives. They filter clean air, provide fresh drinking water, help (2)______ climate change and create homes for thousands of species of plants and animals. (3)________ a billion trees can help save the Earth from climate change and biodiversity loss. When we restore and (4)_______ critical forests, we remove carbon and support biodiversity. A billion is a big number, but we know we can do it together. (5)________ the planet by planting your tree today. This can protect and restore forests for future.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sustain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is in **"(5)________ the planet by planting your tree today." The correct word is "Sustain", meaning to keep something going, or to maintain something in good condition over time. "Sustain the planet"** means to keep the planet healthy/liveable for the future, matching the passage's closing message about protecting and restoring forests "for future".

• Rule — Contextual word choice: The chosen word must match the overall tone and meaning of the passage — here, a call to action to protect/maintain the environment long-term.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Denigrate" is incorrect; it means to criticise unfairly or belittle, which is the opposite of the passage's positive, protective tone.

• Option 2: "Complement" is incorrect; it means to complete or go well with something, which does not fit the instruction to act on the planet.

• Option 4: "Supplement" is incorrect; it means to add something extra to, which does not match the sense of maintaining the planet as a whole.

NOTE

• Sustain is a key word in environmental vocabulary, related to "sustainable" and "sustainability", both frequently tested in SSC comprehension/cloze passages.

• Do not confuse complement (to complete/enhance) with compliment (praise) — a common SSC spelling/vocabulary trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
He has grown into a beautiful youth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. into a handsome youth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a male (a "youth", i.e., a young man) who has developed physically. In English, "handsome" is the conventional adjective used to describe good looks in a man/boy, while "beautiful" is conventionally used for a woman/girl (or for non-human things). The underlined segment must therefore be corrected to "into a handsome youth".

• Rule — Gender-appropriate adjectives of appearance: handsome (for males), beautiful/pretty (for females); good-looking and attractive can be used for either.

• The preposition "into" is correct with the verb "grow" in the sense of transformation/development — "grow into something" means to develop or change into that state over time. It must be retained, not dropped or changed to "in".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in a beautiful youth" is incorrect; it wrongly uses "in" instead of "into", and also wrongly retains "beautiful" for a male subject.

• Option 2: "a beautiful youth" is incorrect; it drops the necessary preposition "into" altogether, breaking the phrasal verb "grow into", and also wrongly retains "beautiful".

• Option 3: "in a handsome youth" is incorrect; although it correctly changes "beautiful" to "handsome", it wrongly uses "in" instead of "into".

NOTE

• Grow into = to develop into (a state); grow up = to become an adult; grow out of = to become too big/old for something (e.g., "he has grown out of his shoes").

• Similar gender-specific word pairs often tested by SSC: handsome/beautiful, bridegroom/bride, bachelor/spinster, actor/actress.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Venom
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Poison.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Venom" means a poisonous substance secreted by animals such as snakes, scorpions, or bees, typically injected by a bite or sting; it is also used figuratively to mean intense malice or hatred. (विष/ज़हर)
◦ Example: The venom of a cobra can be fatal if not treated quickly.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Poison", a general term for any substance capable of causing illness or death when introduced into the body. (ज़हर)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Butter" (मक्खन): a soft fatty food product made from milk/cream; unrelated in meaning to "venom".

• Option 3: "Fruit juice" (फलों का रस): the liquid extracted from fruit; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Honey" (शहद): a sweet substance made by bees; in fact almost opposite in connotation to "venom" (which bees also produce, ironically, in the form of sting venom).

NOTE

• Related words: venomous (adjective, poisonous), toxin (poisonous substance produced by a living organism), antidote (a remedy to counteract poison).

• Do not confuse venom (poison, especially from a bite/sting) with venue (the place where an event happens) — a common SSC spelling trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The inspector smile after he was finished and patted Margie's head.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. smiled.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a completed past action, confirmed by the other verbs in the sentence — "was finished" and "patted" — both of which are in the Simple Past Tense. For grammatical consistency, the underlined verb "smile" must also be in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Tense consistency: When a sentence contains multiple actions that occurred at the same past time, all the main verbs describing those actions should be in the same tense (here, Simple Past). The correct form of "smile" is "smiled".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution required" is incorrect; "smile" is the base form and cannot correctly stand as the main verb in this past-tense sentence.

• Option 3: "was smiled" is incorrect; "smile" is an intransitive verb (it does not take a direct object), so it cannot be used in the passive voice.

• Option 4: "has smiled" is incorrect; the Present Perfect Tense does not match the clearly past-time narrative established by "was finished" and "patted".

NOTE

• Intransitive verbs like smile, laugh, cry, arrive, sleep cannot be used in the passive voice because they have no object to become the subject.

• Always check the tense of the surrounding verbs in a sentence to determine the correct tense of the underlined/blank verb — this is one of the most frequently tested SSC error-types.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
Rohit is write to them three times.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Rohit has written.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contains the phrase "three times", which indicates a repeated action completed up to the present moment, with the possibility of continuing. This is a classic marker of the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense: Subject + has/have + V3 (past participle). Since "Rohit" is third-person singular, the correct auxiliary is "has", and the verb "write" takes its past participle form "written". Correct form: "Rohit has written to them three times."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Rohit was beings written" is incorrect; it is ungrammatical ("beings" is not a verb form) and wrongly uses the passive voice for what should be an active statement.

• Option 2: "Rohit was write" is incorrect; "was" cannot be directly followed by the base form "write".

• Option 3: "Rohit had write" is incorrect; the Past Perfect auxiliary "had" must be followed by a past participle ("written"), not the base form "write", and Past Perfect is not appropriate here as there is no earlier past reference point.

NOTE

• Time expressions such as "three times", "so far", "already", "just", "yet", "since", "for" typically signal the Present Perfect Tense.

• Common irregular past participles frequently tested by SSC: write–wrote–written, break–broke–broken, choose–chose–chosen, speak–spoke–spoken.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Where the shoe pinches
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Where the difficulty lies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Where the shoe pinches" means the exact point or source of a problem or difficulty, especially one that is personally felt but not obvious to others. (कठिनाई का असली कारण/जड़)
◦ Example: Only after losing his job did he realise where the shoe pinches — he had no savings at all.

• The idiom draws on the image of a shoe that looks fine from the outside but causes pain only to the person wearing it — just as only the person facing a problem truly knows its exact cause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Unknown paths" (अज्ञात रास्ते): refers to unfamiliar routes or ventures; unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 2: "Difficult roads" (कठिन रास्ते): a literal description of tough terrain, not the figurative meaning intended.

• Option 4: "Where the shoe hurts": a near-literal restatement of the idiom's words rather than its actual figurative meaning, and is therefore a distractor, not the meaning.

NOTE

• Other footwear-related idioms tested by SSC: "To be in someone's shoes" (to be in their situation), "To fill someone's shoes" (to successfully take over their role), "The boot is on the other foot" (the situation has reversed).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Callous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Cruel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Callous" means emotionally hardened, unfeeling, or showing no sympathy for the suffering of others. (निर्दयी/कठोर हृदय वाला)
◦ Example: His callous remarks about the accident victims shocked everyone present.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Cruel", meaning deliberately causing pain or showing no concern for the suffering of others. (क्रूर)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Generous" (उदार): willing to give freely; the opposite of the unfeeling sense of "callous".

• Option 3: "Affectionate" (स्नेही): showing warmth and fondness; opposite in meaning to "callous".

• Option 4: "Exhausting" (थका देने वाला): causing great tiredness; unrelated to the emotional hardness meant by "callous".

NOTE

• Words with a similar sense of emotional hardness: heartless, unfeeling, insensitive, indifferent, apathetic.

• "Callous" originally referred to hardened skin (a callus); the figurative sense of emotional hardness developed from this literal meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The CEO called for compulsory participation from each employee.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Voluntary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Compulsory" means required by law or a rule; obligatory, something one must do. (अनिवार्य)
◦ Example: Wearing a helmet is compulsory for all two-wheeler riders.

• Its opposite among the options is "Voluntary", meaning done, given, or acting of one's own free will, without being forced. (स्वैच्छिक)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Compliantly" (आज्ञाकारी ढंग से): an adverb meaning "in an obedient manner"; it is not even the same part of speech as the required antonym and does not mean the opposite of "compulsory".

• Option 3: "Obligatory" (अनिवार्य): a synonym of "compulsory", not an antonym.

• Option 4: "Overtly" (खुले तौर पर): means "openly, not secretly"; unrelated to the compulsory/voluntary distinction.

NOTE

• Other synonym–antonym pairs frequently tested: mandatory (syn.) vs voluntary/optional (ant.) for "compulsory".

• Always check that the option you choose matches the correct part of speech (adjective, in this case) as the underlined word — mismatched parts of speech, like Option 2 here, are common SSC distractors.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Baffle
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Confuse.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Baffle" means to completely confuse or perplex someone, especially so that they cannot understand or explain something. (भ्रमित करना/हैरान करना)
◦ Example: The complicated instructions baffled most of the new employees.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Confuse", meaning to cause someone to be unable to think clearly or understand something. (भ्रमित करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Explicate" (स्पष्ट करना): means to explain something in detail, making it clearer — the opposite of confusing someone.

• Option 3: "Barbarous" (क्रूर/असभ्य): means savagely cruel or uncivilised; unrelated to confusion.

• Option 4: "Equalise" (बराबर करना): means to make equal; unrelated in meaning to "baffle".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "baffle": perplex, bewilder, puzzle, mystify, confound.

• Do not confuse baffle (to confuse) with muffle (to deaden sound) — the words look and sound similar but mean very different things.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Logical
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Illogical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Logical" means characterised by clear, sound reasoning; following the rules of logic. (तार्किक)
◦ Example: Her argument was logical and well-supported by evidence.

• Its direct opposite among the options is "Illogical", meaning lacking sense or sound reasoning; not logical. (अतार्किक)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Subtle" (सूक्ष्म): means delicate or not obvious; unrelated to logic or reasoning.

• Option 2: "Random" (यादृच्छिक): means done or occurring without a definite plan or pattern; while a random statement could lack logic, "random" itself is not the standard antonym of "logical".

• Option 3: "Reasonable" (उचित/तर्कसंगत): is close in meaning to "logical" (a near-synonym), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs built with the negative prefix "il-": legal/illegal, legible/illegible, literate/illiterate.

• The prefix "il-" (a variant of "in-") is used before words beginning with "l"; similarly, "im-" is used before m/p (immature, impossible) and "ir-" before r (irregular, irrational).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The company's __________ commitment to sustainability is admirable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. strong.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the company's "commitment to sustainability", which the sentence calls "admirable". This tells us the missing adjective must convey a firm, positive degree of commitment. "Strong commitment" is the standard, natural collocation used to describe a firm, deeply-held commitment worthy of admiration.

• Rule — Positive collocation: The adjective chosen to modify "commitment" must be positive and must collocate naturally with "commitment" in standard English usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "shakeable" is incorrect; it means capable of being shaken or weakened, which contradicts the idea of an admirable, firm commitment.

• Option 2: "resolute" is not strictly ungrammatical here, but "strong commitment" is the far more common, natural collocation used in this exact context (especially in corporate/sustainability writing), which is why it is the most appropriate choice as the question requires.

• Option 3: "wavering" is incorrect; it means uncertain or hesitant, which is the opposite of a commitment worthy of admiration.

NOTE

• Common positive collocations with "commitment": strong commitment, firm commitment, unwavering commitment, deep commitment.

• Common negative collocations to recognise as wrong answers: shaky/wavering/half-hearted commitment.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
To submit a report / on the recent fire accident, / a high level commitee / has been formed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a high level commitee.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "commitee" is misspelled. The correct spelling is "committee" — a group of people appointed for a specific function.
◦ Example: A high-level committee has been formed to investigate the incident.

• Spelling key: COMM + IT + TEE — note the double "m" and the double "t" (com-mit-tee), both of which are commonly dropped by mistake. The word comes from the verb commit, and adds the suffix "-tee", doubling the final consonant of "commit" before the suffix.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To submit a report" is correctly spelled.

• Option 2: "has been formed." is correctly spelled.

• Option 3: "on the recent fire accident," is correctly spelled.

NOTE

• Other frequently misspelled double-letter words tested by SSC: accommodate, embarrass, occurrence, recommend, necessary, possession.

• Memory tip for "committee": it has three double letters — mm, tt, ee — remembered by many as "a committee needs double support".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.
Mala _____________ by cheating on the exam to win her bet with Priya.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. hit below the belt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to hit below the belt" means to act unfairly, dishonestly, or cruelly, especially by taking advantage in a way that is considered against the rules. (गलत/अनुचित तरीके से काम करना)
◦ Example: Cheating on the exam to win the bet was a clear case of Mala hitting below the belt.

• The idiom originates from boxing, where hitting an opponent below the waist belt is against the rules and considered a foul, unfair blow.

• Since the sentence needs the past tense to match "cheating ... to win her bet", the correct form used is "hit below the belt" (hit being both the base and past form of the verb "hit").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "get the sack" (नौकरी से निकाला जाना): means to be dismissed from a job; unrelated to cheating in an exam.

• Option 2: "look down upon" (तुच्छ समझना): means to regard someone as inferior; it does not fit the action of cheating described here.

• Option 4: "fell out" (झगड़ा हो जाना): means to quarrel or have a falling-out with someone; it describes a relationship breakdown, not the act of cheating itself.

NOTE

• Other sports-derived idioms common in SSC exams: "to move the goalposts" (to unfairly change the rules), "a level playing field" (fair conditions for all), "to throw in the towel" (to give up).

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence and select the option with the correct spelling.
Stomach sleepers were rated as being more gregairious and uncomfortable with criticism.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. gregarious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "gregairious" in the given sentence is misspelled. The correct spelling is "gregarious" — meaning fond of the company of others; sociable.
◦ Example: Despite being a stomach sleeper, she was known to be a gregarious and friendly person.

• Spelling key: GREG + ARI + OUS. Note the sequence "a-r-i" (not "a-i-r" as in the misspelling "gregairious"). The word comes from the Latin grex/gregis, meaning "flock" or "herd".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "criticicm" is itself misspelled; the correct spelling is "criticism" (ends in "-cism", not "-cicm"), and in any case the word "criticism" in the original sentence was already spelled correctly.

• Option 3: "ratedd" is itself misspelled; the correct spelling is "rated" (single "d"), and the word "rated" in the original sentence was already spelled correctly.

• Option 4: "stomac" is itself misspelled; the correct spelling is "stomach" (ends in "-ach"), and the word "stomach" in the original sentence was already spelled correctly.

NOTE

• The adjective form is gregarious; the related noun is gregariousness.

• Other commonly confused "-ous" ending words: spontaneous, courteous, curious, tedious, ambiguous — always double-check the vowel sequence before "-ous".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
We are decorate the living-room at the moment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. We are decorating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "at the moment" indicates an action that is happening right now, which requires the Present Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense: Subject + am/is/are + V1 + -ing. Since the subject is "We", the correct auxiliary is "are", and the verb "decorate" must take its -ing form: "decorating". Correct form: "We are decorating the living-room at the moment."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "We are being decorating" is incorrect; "being" is unnecessary here — "being + V-ing" is not a valid English structure — and the sentence should simply be the active present continuous, not a passive-sounding construction.

• Option 2: "We are being decorate" is incorrect for the same reason, and additionally uses the wrong base form "decorate" after "being".

• Option 3: "We are decorates" is incorrect; the auxiliary "are" cannot be followed by the third-person singular form "decorates".

NOTE

• Time expressions such as "at the moment", "now", "currently", "at present", "right now" are strong indicators of the Present Continuous Tense.

• Avoid the common SSC trap of inserting "being" unnecessarily; "being" is correctly used only in passive continuous constructions (e.g., "The room is being decorated") or before an adjective (e.g., "He is being rude").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The perfume she uses has a strong __________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. scent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Scent" means a distinctive smell, especially a pleasant one, such as that of a perfume. Since the sentence talks about a perfume having a **"strong ______", the correct word is "scent", meaning fragrance/smell.
◦ Example:** The rose garden was filled with a sweet scent.

• "Scent", "sent" and "cent" are homophones (words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings), a category frequently tested by SSC.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sent" is the past tense/past participle of the verb "send" (e.g., "I sent the letter"); it does not mean fragrance.

• Option 3: "cent" refers to a unit of currency (one-hundredth of a dollar/rupee) or a mark of measurement (per cent); it is unrelated to smell.

• Option 4: "send" is the base form of the verb meaning to cause something to go somewhere; it is a verb, not a noun that can follow "a strong", and is unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Common homophone sets tested by SSC: scent/sent/cent, their/there/they're, its/it's, peace/piece, principal/principle.

• A quick way to remember: "scent" has a silent "c" and relates to smell (think s-c-ent = fragrance); "cent" relates to money (think cent = currency).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Rosy and Nicky couldn't provide any evidence to support _________ arguments.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. their.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is immediately followed by the noun "arguments", so a possessive adjective (a determiner that modifies a noun) is required, not a pronoun or a homophone with a different function. "Their" correctly shows possession — the arguments belonging to Rosy and Nicky.

• Rule — Possessive adjective vs other forms: A possessive adjective (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) is always followed directly by a noun (their arguments); a possessive pronoun (mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs) stands alone, replacing a noun phrase entirely and is never followed by another noun.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "there" is incorrect; "there" refers to a place or is used to introduce existence ("there is/are"), and cannot modify the noun "arguments".

• Option 2: "theirs" is incorrect; "theirs" is a possessive pronoun that must stand alone (e.g., "The arguments were theirs"), and cannot be directly followed by the noun "arguments".

• Option 4: "they're" is incorrect; it is a contraction of "they are" and makes no grammatical sense before the noun "arguments".

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone set: their (possessive adjective), there (place/existential), they're (contraction of "they are") — one of the most frequently tested SSC error types.

• Similarly confused pair: its (possessive adjective) vs it's (contraction of "it is/it has").
